The stress-strain curve in the new code differs from that of BS8110/BS3400 in

the following two ways:

(a) The initial gradient of the curve (ie. £,) has been changed to match with the
generally lower elastic modulus of the local concrete.

(b) The reduction of the ultimate concrete strain «,, (the strain at the extreme
compression fibre when the concrete fails) with the increase of the concrete
strength f,, to beyond 60 N/mm* has been taken into account so as to
extend the applicability of the curve to high-strength concrete.

However, although Table 3.2 has been referred to for the evaluation of the initial
gradient £,, the method of applying the material safety factor », has not been

specified. In theory, the material safety factor should be applied before
evaluating the initial gradient using either Table 3.2 or Equation 3.1 of the code.
Since after application of the material safety factor, the concrete strength
becomes jf, /y, and is no longer a whole number, it should be better to use

Equation 3.1, which after the material safety factor is applied, becomes:

The value of the ultimate concrete strain ¢,, has to be reduced when the concrete
strength f., is higher than 60 Nimm? because high-strength concrete generally
has a stress-strain curve that would, after reaching the peak, decline more rapidly
than in normal-strength conerete (high-strength concrete is more brittle). To
allow for such effect, the cade has provided the following formula for the
evaluation of «,,:

£,, = 0.0035 for f,, = 60 Nimm?

This formula is based on the research study carried out at The University of Hong

Ho J.C.M., Kwan A.K.H. and Pam H.J., “Ultimate concrete strain and equivalent
rectangular stress block for design of high-strength concrete beams”, Structural
